title: Structs, methods and pointers
summary: Value or pointer receiver, what a capital letter means, and what copying a struct costs you.

concepts.title: Value and pointer receivers
concepts.brief:
A method is a function with a receiver. The receiver can be a **value** or a **pointer**, and the choice decides whether the method can change anything:

- `func (s Store) Add()` — `s` is a fresh copy. Changes to its fields are lost.
- `func (s *Store) Add()` — `s` points at the original. Changes stick.

Calling is forgiving: on an **addressable** value, `store.Add()` compiles for both, because Go inserts `(&store).Add()` for you. That convenience is exactly why the value-receiver bug is so easy to write — the call site looks identical.

The place it stops being forgiving is **interfaces**. The method set of `T` contains only its value-receiver methods; the method set of `*T` contains both. So a `T` does not satisfy an interface whose method has a pointer receiver.

examples.label: Same call site, opposite outcomes
examples.code:
type Counter struct{ n int }

func (c Counter) IncVal()  { c.n++ }   // lost
func (c *Counter) IncPtr() { c.n++ }   // kept

var c Counter
c.IncVal()
c.IncVal()
fmt.Println(c.n)   // 0

c.IncPtr()
fmt.Println(c.n)   // 1   - Go rewrote this as (&c).IncPtr()
examples.note: Nothing at the call site tells you which you got. You have to look at the method.

examples.label: Where the method set bites
examples.code: Buffer does not implement io.Writer (method Write has pointer receiver)
examples.note: The full line begins `cannot use buf (variable of struct type Buffer) as io.Writer value in argument to fmt.Fprintf:` — this is its tail, which is the half that tells you what to do. The fix is almost always `&buf`.

items.prompt: `IncPtr` has a pointer receiver. `c` is a local variable of type `Counter`. Does `c.IncPtr()` compile?
choices: Yes — c is addressable, so Go rewrites it as (&c).IncPtr()
No — you must write (&c).IncPtr() yourself
Yes, but it operates on a copy, so the change is lost
Only if Counter has no value-receiver methods
items.explain: Go takes the address automatically for any addressable value, so both receiver kinds look the same at the call site. The exception is a value that has no address — a map element, or the result of a function call. `m["k"].IncPtr()` does not compile for exactly that reason.

items.prompt: `Write` is defined on `*Buffer`. You pass a `Buffer` value where an `io.Writer` is wanted.

code.label: the tail of the compiler line
code.text: Buffer does not implement io.Writer (method Write has pointer receiver)

choices: Pass `&buf` — only *Buffer's method set includes pointer-receiver methods
Add a value receiver version of Write as well
Convert it: `io.Writer(buf)`
Declare buf with `var buf *Buffer` and leave it nil
items.explain: `&buf`. `*T`'s method set has every method; `T`'s has only the value-receiver ones. The asymmetry exists because Go can always take the address of an addressable variable, but an interface holds a copy, and there would be nothing to take the address *of*. This is the single most common reason a type "mysteriously" fails to implement an interface.

items.prompt: A type has six methods. Five mutate state and need pointer receivers. What should the sixth, a read-only `String()`, use?
choices: A pointer receiver, for consistency across the whole type
A value receiver, since it does not mutate anything
Either — the compiler normalizes them
A value receiver, so it can be called on map elements
items.explain: Mixing receiver kinds on one type is the standard advice to avoid: it makes the method set depend on which method you are reaching for, and `T` ends up satisfying some interfaces while `*T` satisfies others. Pick one per type. If any method needs a pointer, they all take a pointer.

items.prompt: `var c *Counter` — a nil pointer. You call `c.Describe()`, whose body never touches any field. What happens?
choices: It runs fine — a nil pointer receiver is legal until you dereference it
It panics immediately; calling a method on nil is never allowed
It does not compile — nil pointers cannot be receivers
It runs, but the receiver is silently replaced with a zero value
items.explain: Legal. A method call on a nil pointer passes nil as the receiver; it only panics if the body dereferences it. Some types use this deliberately — a nil `*TreeNode` behaving as an empty tree. It also explains a confusing trace: the panic points inside the method, not at the call.

items.prompt: Complete the receiver so `Add` can modify the Counter it is called on: `func (c ____ Counter) Add()`
items.explain: `*Counter` — a pointer receiver. Without the star you get a copy and every mutation is discarded, with no warning from the compiler or `go vet`. If a method's job is to change the receiver, it needs the star.

concepts.title: Capital letters and struct tags
concepts.brief:
Go has no `public` or `private`. An identifier beginning with an **uppercase letter** is visible outside its package; everything else is package-private. That applies to types, functions, methods, constants and struct fields alike.

It is not only about other packages. Anything using **reflection** — `encoding/json`, YAML, `database/sql`, template engines — can only see exported fields. A lowercase field is invisible to all of them, silently.

**Struct tags** are string metadata attached to a field, read at runtime by those same libraries. The compiler does not check them, so a typo in a tag is not an error — it just stops working.

examples.label: What json can and cannot see
examples.note: `-` means never serialize. `omitempty` means skip when the value is the zero value — which is why an explicit `false` or `0` disappears too.

examples.label: The tag is just a string
examples.code:
Name string `json:name`     // missing quotes - silently ignored
Name string `JSON:"name"`   // wrong key - silently ignored
Name string `json:"name"`   // correct
examples.note: `go vet`'s structtag check catches malformed tags and json-tagged unexported fields. It is worth running in CI for this reason alone.

items.prompt: A struct field is `count int` with a `json:"count"` tag. What does `json.Marshal` emit for it?
choices: Nothing — unexported fields are skipped and the tag is ignored
`"count":0` — the tag makes it visible
An error about marshalling an unexported field
`"count":null`
items.explain: Nothing at all, with no error. Reflection cannot read or set unexported fields from outside the declaring package, so `encoding/json` skips them and the tag is dead text. "Why is my JSON empty?" is nearly always a lowercase letter. `go vet` flags this exact case.

items.prompt: Match each json struct tag to what it does.
pairs: Uses "name" as the key instead of the field name
Dropped when the value is its zero value
Uses the exact field name, capital included
items.explain: The leading comma in `",omitempty"` matters — it means "keep the default name, add this option". Write `"omitempty"` without it and you have renamed the field to `omitempty`, which is a real bug people ship.

items.prompt: Which of these are visible to code in another package?
choices: `func Connect()`
`type Config struct`
`func newPool()`
A `Timeout` field inside an unexported type `config`
items.explain: Three of them, and the last is the interesting one. A field is exported on its own first letter, so `Timeout` is exported even though `config` is not. Another package cannot *name* `config`, so it cannot declare one — but if an exported function hands one back, `cfg := pkg.New(); cfg.Timeout` compiles fine. It is also why an unexported type still marshals to JSON perfectly well. Only `newPool` is genuinely out of reach.

items.prompt: `Enabled bool `json:"enabled,omitempty"`` and you set `Enabled = false`. What is in the JSON?
choices: The key is missing — false is the zero value, so omitempty drops it
`"enabled":false`
`"enabled":null`
The key is missing only if the field is also a pointer
items.explain: It vanishes. `omitempty` means "omit when zero", and for a bool that is `false` — so you cannot distinguish "set to false" from "not set". The standard fix is `*bool`, where nil means absent and a pointer to false means explicitly false. The same trap applies to `0` and `""`.

concepts.title: Copying and comparing structs
concepts.brief:
Assigning a struct **copies every field**. Passing one to a function copies it. Storing one in a slice copies it. There are no references unless you use a pointer.

The copy is **shallow**. A slice, map or pointer field is copied as a header or an address, so the copy and the original still share whatever it points at.

`==` works on structs only when **every field is comparable**. A struct containing a slice, a map or a func cannot be compared, and that is a compile error rather than a runtime one. For those, use `reflect.DeepEqual`.

examples.label: Shallow is the word that matters
examples.note: Two fields, two different outcomes, from one assignment. The int was copied; the slice header was copied and still points at the same array.

examples.label: Comparability is checked at compile time
examples.code: ./main.go:14:14: invalid operation: a == b (struct containing []string cannot be compared)
examples.note: Comparable structs can also be used as map keys. One slice field anywhere inside takes both abilities away.

items.prompt: `b := a` where `a` is a struct with an `int` field `N` and a `[]string` field `Tags`. You set `b.N = 2` and `b.Tags[0] = "y"`. What changed in `a`?
choices: Only Tags[0] — the int was copied, the slice's backing array is shared
Both — b is a reference to a
Neither — assignment deep-copies the struct
Only N — slices are copied by value, ints are not
items.explain: The copy is shallow. `N` is an independent int; `Tags` is an independent *header* pointing at the same array. This is why "I passed the struct by value so it is safe" is wrong whenever the struct holds a slice, map, pointer or channel. A deep copy has to be written by hand.

items.prompt: Your struct has a `[]string` field. You write `if a == b`.
choices: Compile error — a struct containing a slice is not comparable
It compiles and compares the slices element by element
It compiles and compares the slice pointers
It compiles but panics at runtime on the slice field
items.explain: `invalid operation: a == b (struct containing []string cannot be compared)`. Slices, maps and funcs are not comparable, and that poisons any struct holding one — it also cannot be a map key. Use `reflect.DeepEqual` for an occasional check, or write an `Equal` method if it is on a hot path, because DeepEqual is slow and reflective.

items.prompt: Your struct embeds a `sync.Mutex`. You pass it to a function by value. `go vet` says: `passes lock by value`. Why does it matter?
choices: The copy has its own lock, so the two copies no longer exclude each other
Copying a locked mutex deadlocks immediately
It is only a style warning; the lock still works
The mutex becomes nil in the copy and panics on Lock
items.explain: You end up with two independent mutexes guarding what you thought was one thing, so the mutual exclusion silently stops working — and it will look fine under light load. A type containing a mutex should always be passed and stored as a pointer. `go vet`'s copylocks check is on by default — but not in the reduced set that `go test` runs, so it only fires when you invoke vet yourself.

items.prompt: Which standard-library function compares two values that contain slices or maps, where `==` will not compile?
items.explain: `reflect.DeepEqual(a, b)`. Two cautions: it is reflective and slow, so keep it out of hot paths and favor it in tests; and it treats a nil slice and an empty non-nil slice as **different**, which surprises people comparing JSON round-trips.

concepts.title: Embedding is not inheritance
concepts.brief:
Declare a field with a type and no name and you have **embedded** it. Its methods and fields are **promoted**: you can call them on the outer type directly.

It looks like inheritance and is not. There is no virtual dispatch. A method on the embedded type that calls another method gets the **embedded type's** version, never an override on the outer type. Promotion is a compile-time shorthand for `outer.Inner.Method()`, nothing more.

Embedding an exported type also exports its methods. Embedding `sync.Mutex` puts `Lock()` and `Unlock()` on your public API, which is usually not what you meant.

examples.label: Promotion
examples.note: This is how `http.ServeMux` and most middleware get composed, and how a type picks up `io.Reader` behavior by embedding something that already has it.

examples.label: Named field vs embedded, for a mutex
examples.note: The standard library embeds it in a few places on purpose. For your own types, a named `mu` field is the safer default.

items.prompt: `Job` embeds `Base`, which has a field `ID`. Which of these compile?
choices: Both `j.ID` and `j.Base.ID`
Only `j.Base.ID` — promotion applies to methods, not fields
Only `j.ID` — the embedded name is not accessible
Neither unless Job declares its own ID field
items.explain: Both. Promotion covers fields and methods, and the long form always remains. If `Job` declared its own `ID`, the outer one would win and `j.Base.ID` would be the only way to reach the inner — shadowing, the same idea as with variables.

items.prompt: `Base.Describe()` calls `b.Label()`. `Job` embeds `Base` and defines its own `Label()`. Which `Name()` runs when you call `job.Describe()`?
choices: Base's — there is no virtual dispatch, so the embedded method never sees Job
Job's — the outer type's method overrides the embedded one
Job's, but only if the method has a pointer receiver
It does not compile; the method name is ambiguous
items.explain: `Base`'s. The receiver inside `Describe` is a `Base` and it knows nothing about any type embedding it. This is the sharpest difference from inheritance, and it bites people porting a template-method pattern from Java or Python. To get polymorphism in Go you pass an **interface**, not an embedded struct.

items.prompt: `job.Thing` — put the steps Go takes to resolve that name in order.
steps: Look for Thing declared directly on Job
If it is not there, look one level in, at the types Job embeds
If exactly one embedded type has it at that depth, promote it
If two embedded types have it at the same depth, the selector is ambiguous and it is a compile error
items.explain: Shallowest wins, and a tie is an error rather than a choice. That is the whole mechanism: a field on the outer type shadows a promoted one, and embedding two types that both have `Close()` compiles happily until the day you actually call `x.Close()`. Writing `x.Inner.Close()` is how you break the tie.

items.prompt: What does embedding `sync.Mutex` into your exported struct do to its API?
choices: It promotes Lock and Unlock, so any caller can lock your type
Nothing; promoted methods stay package-private
It makes the struct uncopyable, enforced by the compiler
It is required for the mutex to protect the other fields
items.explain: `Lock()` and `Unlock()` become part of your public API, and callers can hold your lock — or deadlock you. Use a named `mu sync.Mutex` field unless you specifically want to expose locking. Note too that embedding a mutex makes the struct unsafe to copy, which `go vet`'s copylocks check will tell you about.

items.prompt: `type Service struct { io.Reader }` — embedding an *interface* rather than a struct. Which are true?
choices: Service satisfies io.Reader, because Read is promoted
The embedded Reader is nil until you assign one
Calling Read on a Service with a nil embedded Reader panics
It does not compile; only structs can be embedded
items.explain: All but the last — interfaces can be embedded, and it is a genuinely useful trick: your type satisfies the interface immediately while implementing only the methods it wants to change, delegating the rest. The cost is that the zero value is a nil interface and every unimplemented method panics at runtime instead of failing to compile.
